entries.title: Single
entries.text:
Single

clean singledirty single

A single, in single shot cinematography, is a coverage shot of one principal character, not a one-take scene. A clean single keeps other bodies out; a dirty single lets a shoulder or blur from the partner chew the edge without becoming a true over-the-shoulder.

Create this Single

Narrative function

A single isolates. The other person can still be in the room, but they no longer author the frame.

This is how you make someone alone during a conversation, or how you give a listener a private beat. It is not a oner and not a long take; those are duration.

A single is occupancy: one principal. It is the wrong tool when the relationship must stay visible as a shoulder or as a shared two-shot.

Going to singles too early turns every scene into ping-pong. Going to a clean single at the right time can feel like the partner has been erased.

How it works

Frame one person. For a clean single, keep edges empty of the partner (Clean Frame).

For a dirty single, allow a sliver of the other body as edge chew (Dirty Frame) without a composed foreground shoulder. Size is often Close-Up or Medium Close-Up, but a single can be a medium of one.

Prompt: Clean single of [Subject], one person, no foreground shoulder, the frame belonging entirely to them.

When to use it

Use it to isolate: the other person is gone even if they are in the room. Do not leave a stray composed shoulder if you meant clean, and do not call a continuous long take a single just because one actor walks.

Compared with similar shots

Over-the-shoulder coverage uses the partner as a foreground anchor. A Two-Shot keeps both principals.

A Close-Up is a size a single often uses. A Oner is a long unbroken take, a different word.

Single means one occupant of the shot.

Close-UpRead micro-expression. Default for important dialogue.

Over-the-Shoulder CoverageDefault dialogue coverage with spatial glue.

Extreme Close-UpA detail is the scene: an eye, a mouth, a trigger.

In film

The Silence of the Lambs uses clean, frontal singles in the interviews so the glass and the partner can vanish and the face owns the rectangle. That isolation is the coverage choice.

Grammar: one person, the rest of the relationship offscreen.

Prompt it

Say one person and whether the edges are clean. Example: Clean single of [Subject], one person, no foreground shoulder, the frame belonging entirely to them.

If you want dirty, say a blur of the partner at the frame edge, not an OTS shoulder. For video, do not let a second face walk in unless that is the beat.

Use in Image Generator

Clean single of [Subject], one person, no foreground shoulder, the frame belonging entirely to them.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is Over-the-Shoulder Coverage (composed near shoulder) or a Two-Shot. The tell is a sharp second face, or a textbook OTS.

Another tell is calling a oner a single. Fix: one principal, decide clean or dirty, do not confuse occupancy with duration.

Questions

What is Single in film?

A single is a shot containing one principal character. Clean singles keep other bodies out; dirty singles let a bit of the partner chew the edge. It is coverage occupancy, not a synonym for a one-take scene.

Single vs Over-the-Shoulder Coverage

OTS keeps a near shoulder or head as a compositional foreground while we watch the far face. A single removes that anchor so the frame belongs to one person. A dirty single is still a single; it is not a full OTS unless the near body is the viewpoint fragment.

When should I use Single?

Use it to isolate someone during or after a conversation. Do not jump there so early that the relationship never exists in frame, and do not confuse it with a oner.

How do I prompt Single for AI image or video?

Write Clean single of [Subject], one person, no foreground shoulder. If you want dirty, specify a sliver of another body at the edge. Keep a second face out of the shot.

entries.title: Cut-ins
entries.text:
Cut-ins

cut in

A cut-in, or cut in shot, moves from a wider view to a closer detail of something already present in that space, usually along the same axis. It proves a fact the wide cannot prove: the hands, the phone, the wound.

Create this Cut-ins

Narrative function

The master already showed the table. The cut-in shows the text on the phone, the blood at the cuff, the grip on the glass.

Because the object was in the wider shot, the audience does not feel teleported. They feel informed.

It is the wrong tool when the detail was never in the geography (a sudden letter from nowhere) or when you leave the action for a clock on another wall. Those are insert-as-new-object and cutaway.

A cut-in is tighter, same world, same beat, often the same lens axis.

How it works

From the Master Shot or a wider size, punch in on a detail that was already visible, keeping screen direction and roughly the same camera axis. An Axial Cut is the hard version of this: a jump along the lens axis.

Match key side. Prompt: Cut-in on a detail of [Subject] already in the master, tighter, the same axis, a fact the wide cannot prove.

When to use it

Use it to show the hands, the phone, the wound that the wide already contained but could not prove. Do not change axis so violently that it reads as a new setup, and do not cut in on an object that was not there.

Compared with similar shots

An Insert Shot may introduce a plot object in close view; a cut-in tightens on what the wide already had. A Cutaway leaves the primary action.

An Axial Cut is the editorial jump along the axis; cut-ins are the tighter shots you land on. An Extreme Close-Up may be the size of the cut-in, but ECU is the crop, not the coverage move.

Insert ShotPoint at the thing that will matter later.

Axial CutChange shot size without changing angle.

Extreme Close-UpA detail is the scene: an eye, a mouth, a trigger.

In film

Classical coverage is built on this grammar: master, then cut in to the business that the master only implied. You see it whenever a wide conversation yields a closer pair of hands without leaving the table.

Use that as the rule, not as a specific poster frame.

Prompt it

Say already in the master and same axis. Example: Cut-in on a detail of [Subject] already in the master, tighter, the same axis, a fact the wide cannot prove.

Name the detail (hands, phone, wound). For video, do not relocate the camera around the table; you are closer on the same line.

Use in Image Generator

Cut-in on a detail of [Subject] already in the master, tighter, the same axis, a fact the wide cannot prove.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is a Cutaway (you left) or an Insert Shot of a new object. The tell is a different wall, a new prop, or a reverse angle pretending to be a punch-in.

Fix: same space, same axis, tighter on a fact that was already there.

Questions

What is Cut-ins in film?

A cut-in is a closer shot of a detail that already exists in a wider view of the same space, often on the same axis. It shows the hands, the phone, or the wound the wide could not prove.

Cut-ins vs Insert Shot

An insert is a designed close view of a story detail, which may or may not have been readable in the master. A cut-in specifically tightens on something already in that wider shot. If the object appears from nowhere, you are inserting, not cutting in.

When should I use Cut-ins?

Use it when the wide has the geography and you need the small fact. Do not use it to leave the scene, and do not use it to introduce a prop that was not there.

How do I prompt Cut-ins for AI image or video?

Write Cut-in on a detail of [Subject] already in the master, tighter, the same axis, and name the fact. Keep the same key and geography as the wide.

entries.title: Gesture
entries.text:
Gesture

Gesture cinematography sizes and times a shot around a discrete expressive body movement: a hand, a glance, a weight shift. The plot is in the motion, not in an object sitting still.

Create this Gesture

Narrative function

Sometimes the scene is not the face and not the prop, but the almost-touch, the glove tightening, the look that does not land. Gesture coverage treats that small action as the beat.

Duration matters: the movement has a start, a peak, and a settle. It is the wrong tool when the object is the fact (a key, a letter) rather than what the body does.

It is also the wrong tool as a wide master where fingers die in the noise of a room. Get close enough that the motion reads, then let it finish.

How it works

Frame for the moving part. Hands often want a close crop without becoming a product shot; a glance may live in a Close-Up of the eyes.

Keep the body connected enough that the motion has a source (wrist, shoulder). Light to separate fingers from background.

Prompt: Gesture close on [Subject], the meaning in a hand, a glance, a weight shift, coverage of the small action.

When to use it

Use it when the plot is in the fingers: an almost-touch in a corridor, a glove, a glass that does not quite rise. Do not cover it so wide the motion dies, and do not freeze it into an object insert.

Compared with similar shots

An Insert Shot is usually the object as fact. A Close-Up is a size that may hold a gesture, or may hold a still face.

An Extreme Close-Up can be a fingertip as texture rather than as action. Gesture means the expressive movement is the subject.

If nothing moves, you probably wanted an insert.

Insert ShotPoint at the thing that will matter later.

Close-UpRead micro-expression. Default for important dialogue.

Extreme Close-UpA detail is the scene: an eye, a mouth, a trigger.

In film

In the Mood for Love builds withheld romance out of hands, glances, and slow weight shifts more than out of speeches. Drive lets gloves, a wheel, and small body decisions carry threat.

Grammar: the small action is the line.

Prompt it

Name the movement. Example: Gesture close on [Subject], the meaning in a hand, a glance, a weight shift, coverage of the small action.

Say what the body does (fingers almost touching, a look away). For video, one motion with a settle; do not add a camera tour.

Use in Image Generator

Gesture close on [Subject], the meaning in a hand, a glance, a weight shift, coverage of the small action.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is an Insert Shot of a still object, or a Close-Up of a face that never moves. The tell is a static prop hero, or a wide where the hand is a blur.

Fix: size to the moving part, let the action complete.

Questions

What is Gesture in film?

Gesture coverage is a shot sized and timed for a discrete expressive body movement: a hand, a glance, a shift of weight. The meaning is the action, not a still object and not a wide master of the room.

Gesture vs Insert Shot

An insert shows a story object or detail, often still enough to read as a fact. Gesture shows what a body does with or without that object. A key in the palm can be an insert; the hesitation before the hand closes is gesture.

When should I use Gesture?

Use it when the beat is a small body action the wide cannot prove. Do not use it for a still product-like object, and do not bury the motion in a master.

Write Gesture close on [Subject], and name the hand, glance, or weight shift. For video, describe one motion and a settle. Keep the camera still unless the technique is a move.

entries.title: Interview
entries.text:
Interview

Interview cinematography is a talking-head setup: stable size, eyeline just off the lens, a listener implied. Someone is answering a question we often do not hear.

Create this Interview

Narrative function

An interview frame is not merely an MCU. It is a social geometry: the subject speaks to a person beside the camera, look space opens toward that listener, and the audience sits in on an answered question.

Direct address into the lens is a different contract (confession, host, warning). It is the wrong tool when two fictional characters are in a scene together and you needed OTS or a two-shot.

It is also the wrong tool if the eyeline hits the glass and you did not mean to break the fourth wall. Keep the size stable; hunting around the face turns testimony into a music video.

How it works

Size usually Medium Close-Up or a loose Close-Up. Camera at Eye Level.

Eyeline a few degrees off lens, toward an implied interviewer. Give Look Space on the look side.

Motivated, simple key; catchlight in the eyes. Prompt: Interview frame of [Subject], talking-head distance, eyeline just off lens, a listener implied.

When to use it

Use it when someone is answering a question we did not hear: documentary testimony, a fake-doc confession, a talking-head insert in a drama. Do not put the eyeline into the lens unless you mean direct address, and do not use this grammar for a two-person scene that should be OTS.

Compared with similar shots

A Medium Close-Up is only a crop; interview is the off-lens eyeline plus implied listener. Eye level is the height.

Over-the-Shoulder would show the questioner. A video portrait holds a face as a study, often without the Q&A contract.

Interview means testimony geometry.

Medium Close-UpTalk without losing body language.

Eye LevelDefault honesty. Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

Extreme Close-UpA detail is the scene: an eye, a mouth, a trigger.

In film

The Fog of War parks a speaker in this grammar so policy becomes a face answering questions. Many social-issue films borrow the same talking-head language (including The Social Dilemma's interview mode): stable size, off-lens eyeline, a listener we take on faith.

Grammar: someone is being asked.

Prompt it

Lock eyeline and size. Example: Interview frame of [Subject], talking-head distance, eyeline just off lens, a listener implied.

Specify look space toward camera-left or camera-right. For video, hold; small hand motion is fine.

Do not stare down the lens unless you want direct address.

Use in Image Generator

Interview frame of [Subject], talking-head distance, eyeline just off lens, a listener implied.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is a generic Medium Close-Up with eyes into the lens, or an Over-the-Shoulder Coverage of a scene. The tell is a host stare, or a second character in a fictional blocking.

Fix: off-lens eyeline, implied listener, stable talking-head size.

Questions

What is Interview in film?

Interview cinematography is a talking-head setup in which the subject answers an offscreen questioner. Size is stable, the eyeline sits just off the lens, and a listener is implied even if we never see them.

Interview vs Medium Close-Up

MCU is a chest-up crop that can be used for any dialogue. Interview is a setup: off-lens eyeline, look space toward a questioner, testimony as the job. You can shoot an MCU that is not an interview, and an interview that is slightly tighter or looser than MCU.

When should I use Interview?

Use it for testimony, documentary talking heads, or a drama that borrows that contract. Do not use it when two characters should share a scene in OTS, and do not aim the eyes at the lens unless you mean direct address.

How do I prompt Interview for AI image or video?

Write Interview frame of [Subject], talking-head distance, eyeline just off lens, a listener implied. Add look space and eye-level. For video, hold the size; do not tour the room.

entries.title: Product
entries.text:
Product

Product cinematography lights and frames an object the way a portrait treats a face: hero angle, catalog clarity, controlled reflections. The thing is the subject, not a plot insert in a messy room.

Create this Product

Narrative function

A product frame sells readability: logo plane, material, edges, how metal and glass behave. Speculars are designed, not accidental.

The background is often a sweep, a void, or a set built to disappear. It is the wrong tool when the object is a story fact inside a scene (a bloody letter on a kitchen table).

That is an insert, and it should keep the room's key. It is also the wrong tool if the camera orbits so fast the form never settles.

Show the object; let a Lazy Susan turn it if every side must read.

How it works

Choose a hero three-quarter or a true elevation. Large soft sources for wrapping highlights; flags and cards to kill ugly speculars on chrome.

Macro only for texture. A turntable or a slow orbit is a separate move.

Prompt: Product hero of [Subject], catalog clarity, controlled reflections, the object as the only subject.

When to use it

Use it to sell the thing by lighting it like a face: a phone, a bottle, a watch on a sweep. Do not use drama-insert mess if you need catalog clarity, and do not use this glamour on a plot object that should look found.

Compared with similar shots

An Insert Shot lives in scene coverage as a plot fact, matching the room. Macro is an optic for small texture, which a product shot may use.

A Lazy Susan is a rotation method. Product is the commercial portrait job: controlled reflections, hero angle, the object as subject.

MacroThe plot is microscopic.

Lazy SusanShow an object or costume from every side.

Extreme Close-UpA detail is the scene: an eye, a mouth, a trigger.

In film

Commercials and Apple keynotes are the public grammar: one object, clean plane, designed highlights, no accidental kitchen mess. Feature films sometimes steal this for a fetishized prop, which is a choice.

Grammar: catalog clarity, not found-object dirt, unless the brief is worn-in hero.

Prompt it

Name the object as hero. Example: Product hero of [Subject], catalog clarity, controlled reflections, the object as the only subject.

Specify material (brushed aluminum, glass, leather) and the background (black sweep, white cyclorama). For video, one slow turn or a locked hero; do not add a person unless they are a scale hand.

Use in Image Generator

Product hero of [Subject], catalog clarity, controlled reflections, the object as celebrity.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is an Insert Shot in dirty scene light, or a Macro texture with no hero angle. The tell is leftover room clutter, or a smear of uncontrolled speculars.

Fix: isolate the object, design the highlights, pick a hero angle.

Questions

What is Product in film?

Product cinematography frames and lights an object as the subject, with catalog clarity and controlled reflections, the way a portrait treats a face. It is a commercial or hero-object job, not a synonym for any close-up of a thing.

Product vs Insert Shot

An insert is a story detail inside a scene, usually matching that scene's light. A product shot isolates the object as a hero, often on a sweep or void, with designed speculars. A bloody envelope on a table is an insert; a phone on black acrylic is product.

When should I use Product?

Use it when the object must read as a designed hero. Do not use it for a plot fact that should stay in the room, and do not let reflections go unmanaged on chrome and glass.

How do I prompt Product for AI image or video?

Write Product hero of [Subject], catalog clarity, controlled reflections, the object as the only subject. Name materials and background. For video, a slow turntable or a locked hero beat.

entries.title: Video Portraits
entries.text:
Video Portraits

A video portrait is a sustained, simply covered study of one person: stable size, patient time, the face as the whole event. Duration is the intimacy; a person is enough.

Volume

Create this Video Portraits

Narrative function

A video portrait is not a close-up you cut away from after a line. You hold.

Blink, breath, a swallow, the tiny life in the face becomes the content. It sits closer to a painting that is allowed to live than to dialogue coverage.

It is the wrong tool when you need ping-pong coverage, a story insert, or a camera tour of the room. It is also the wrong tool if you freeze everything except one looping element: that is a cinemagraph.

Here the person is alive in small ways, and time is the point.

How it works

Lock the camera. Size a Close-Up or Medium Close-Up.

Light a simple, stable key. Hold long enough that duration registers (several seconds, sometimes much more).

No motivated move unless a tiny push is the brief. Prompt still: Video portrait of [Subject], a held face, duration as intimacy.

Motion brief: A long held portrait of [Subject], tiny life in the face, almost still.

When to use it

Use it when a person is enough: a Screen Test, a study, an almost-still that breathes. Do not add a tour, and do not cut away the moment a thought appears; the hold is the piece.

Compared with similar shots

A Close-Up is a size used inside coverage; it usually leaves. A Cinemagraph freezes most of the image and loops one isolated motion.

A Single is occupancy of one body in scene coverage. A video portrait is duration plus stillness of a person as the entire event.

Interview testimony has a questioner; this may have none.

Close-UpRead micro-expression. Default for important dialogue.

CinemagraphA photograph that refuses to die.

Extreme Close-UpA detail is the scene: an eye, a mouth, a trigger.

In film

Warhol's Screen Tests are the plain grammar: a person, a hold, time doing the work. The Irishman uses long, patient close-ups of faces that are allowed to sit, related in duration if not in art-historical setup.

Grammar: hold the person.

Prompt it

Demand the hold. Still: Video portrait of [Subject], a held face, duration as intimacy.

Video: A long held portrait of [Subject], tiny life in the face, almost still. Forbid camera travel.

Allow blink, breath, a swallow. Do not write cinemagraph unless only one element should move.

Use in Video Generator

A long held portrait of [Subject], tiny life in the face, almost still.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is a dialogue Close-Up that wants a reverse, or a Cinemagraph with a frozen body and a looping steam jet. The tell is a camera move, a cut on a line, or a dead freeze.

Fix: lock off, keep the person slightly alive, hold.

Questions

What is Video Portraits in film?

A video portrait is a sustained study of one person at a stable size, with time itself as the intimacy. The face (or figure) is the whole event, almost still, with only tiny life in the features.

Video Portraits vs Close-Up

A close-up is a crop that often exists to deliver a line or a reaction, then leave. A video portrait uses a similar crop but stays: duration is the point. If you are about to cut to the other person, you are in coverage, not in a portrait study.

When should I use Video Portraits?

Use it when a person is enough and holding is the piece. Do not use it for ordinary shot/reverse, and do not turn it into a looping cinemagraph unless that is the brief.

How do I prompt Video Portraits for AI image or video?

Write Video portrait of [Subject], a held face, duration as intimacy. For motion: A long held portrait of [Subject], tiny life in the face, almost still. Lock the camera. Allow only blink, breath, or a swallow.

entries.title: Wide Shot (WS)
entries.text:
Wide Shot (WS)

wideWSlong shotLS

A wide shot shows the subject in full environment, with bodies small enough that place still speaks. It is environment-forward coverage: do not isolate yet.

Create this Wide Shot

Narrative function

Size is a sentence. A wide shot maps who can reach the door, where the street goes, what weather is doing.

People are in the picture so we know the scale of the place, but the place is still talking. If you isolate too early, the scene loses its map.

It is the wrong tool when the beat is a face, a holster, or a head-to-toe costume portrait. It is also the wrong tool if the human has become an unreadable speck (extreme long shot) or if you only needed to declare the building before the scene (establishing as a job).

Use wide to keep geography in play, then change size when a new fact requires a tighter sentence.

How it works

Keep enough architecture, street, or weather that doors, paths, and weather remain readable. Bodies should not fill the height the way they do in a full-body portrait.

A 24mm in a room or a longer lens across a square can both be wide; the crop is whether place still speaks. Prompt: Wide shot of [Subject] in full environment, bodies small enough that place still speaks.

When to use it

Use it when you must not isolate yet: who can reach the door, how far the platform runs, whether two groups can see each other. Do not crop into a full-body fashion frame and call it wide, and do not use it as a blank postcard with no relation to the scene's paths.

Compared with similar shots

A Full Body makes the complete figure the subject, head to toe, place as a border. A Long Shot is the person-in-world size: full figure plus geography, still a locatable human.

An Extreme Long Shot is speck-scale land. An Establishing Shot is a where-and-when job that often uses a wide.

A Master Shot is the action skeleton, which may be wide if blocking needs it. Wide is the environment-forward coverage attitude, not a synonym for those four.

Long ShotPlace a human in a world that could ignore them.

Establishing ShotOpen a scene. Tell us where and when.

Extreme Long ShotScale is the emotion.

In film

Once Upon a Time in the West lets station and desert speak while bodies remain small enough that place is the sentence. Lawrence of Arabia can sit in this band when geography is still coverage, not yet a speck-scale subject.

Grammar: keep the map; do not portrait.

Prompt it

Say full environment and small bodies. Example: Wide shot of [Subject] in full environment, bodies small enough that place still speaks.

Name the door, the street, the weather. Do not write head to toe hero, mid-thigh cowboy, or speck.

For video, hold the geography; a tiny figure motion is enough.

Use in Image Generator

Wide shot of [Subject] in full environment, bodies small enough that place still speaks.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is a Full Body (person fills the height) or a Long Shot labeled wide with no coverage job. The tell is a costume portrait, or a speck landscape with no scene paths.

Fix: place still speaks, bodies small enough to keep the map, geography that the next cut can use.

Questions

What is Wide Shot in film?

A wide shot shows the subject in a full environment, with bodies small enough that place still speaks. It is environment-forward coverage, not a synonym for full body, long shot, or establishing shot.

Wide Shot vs Full Body

Full body is a complete figure as the subject, head to toe, with environment as a readable border. A wide shot keeps place in charge: doors, streets, and weather remain the sentence, and people are small enough not to isolate yet. If the person fills the frame height, you are in full body, not wide.

When should I use Wide Shot?

Use it when geography must stay in play and you should not isolate yet. Do not use it as a head-to-toe portrait, and do not use it when scale should go to a speck.

How do I prompt Wide Shot for AI image or video?

Write Wide shot of [Subject] in full environment, bodies small enough that place still speaks. Name architecture and weather. Keep people from filling the height of the frame.
